Q: Seeking Roadmap and Advanced Resources for Deepening JavaScript Knowledge A:

There is no way around it, you really need to be/get comfortable - in terms of not even thinking of them anymore as such, but you breathe it/them - with the core features of the language, which are ...

  • functions and closures ... they are both everywhere.

  • delegation - both of its kinds. It forces you to understand "binding", "late binding" and what `this` points to at a given (execution) context.

    • the implicit, prototype-based, automatic delegation mechanism, hence inheritance.

    • explicit delegation via `call` and `apply` and their "lazy" cousin `bind`.

  • `async`/`await` and **`Promise`**s ... do not skip them. They are tremendously useful tools which made JavaScript the modern language it is now. And you need to understand what lies underneath - the event loop, task queue, and microtask queue (which predate Promises and underlie all async behavior, including callbacks and events) - in order to reason about execution order rather than guess at it.

At the same time, you need to accept that class-based inheritance is neither a synonym for, nor does it equal the concept of OOP; it never was/did. OOP is about objects, how they encapsulate data and how they communicate - no classes needed.

Class syntax is a pragmatic tool for the common case, not the conceptual heart of OOP.

Nevertheless, I'm not at all discouraging the usage of class syntax. It's a reasonable default when you need multiple instances of the same shape. And class syntax in JavaScript is not just, as it so often gets (mis)quoted ... "syntactical sugar over prototypes". It reaches beyond that, and it enables/ensures well-structured code-bases and optimized engine-handling/execution.

But in order to "breathe"/"inhale" the language to its fullest, right from the beginning, I suggest two research projects that both target composition; one for object-composition and the other one for function-composition.

You could e.g. try to tackle the domain of object-composition by implementing a function-based mixin that mimics JavaScript's `EventTarget` type (which forces you into a deep-dive into event-systems). And as for the "functional" aspect, I suggest you implement at least one of the two behaviors which both are capable of altering the timing of a function's execution, while said function actually is called repeatedly. Choose either `throttle` or `debounce`, and build it in the form of a function that accepts a function-type parameter along with (an) additional timing parameter/s, and which returns another function that controls the invocation of its consumed function (the one that was passed as argument).

In case that is too much for the beginning, get comfortable first mostly with `Array` methods (of the prototype kind) and with all the static `Object` methods that enable you to build exactly (or close to) the kind of type-systems one preferably does build via class-constructors.

Have a closer look at `WeakMap`s and `WeakSet`s, as well as at `Map` and `Set`. If you are curious enough, make a detour to `Proxy`/ies.

And always remember, `function` is your mightiest tool, for it implements behavior and expresses intent. It's your closest/most valued ally, next to modules and plain objects - where modules are for grouping/managing domain-specific implementations, and plain objects are for grouping/managing pure data.

Q: How to avoid that the first capture group is omitted? A:

All you need here is to replace the ^ anchor with \A.

\A\s+(?<CODE>[X][B|M]\d{6}[A-Z]|[a-z]?)\s+(?<NAME>.+)$

See a regex 101 demo.

Or don't use the multiline mode.

"(?-m)^\s+(?<CODE>[X][B|M]\d{6}[A-Z]|[a-z]?)\s+(?<NAME>.+)"

See a regex 101 demo.
